profile.summary: Amos is a prophetic denunciation of false religiosity and social injustice in Israel. The book shows that correct worship and correct ethics go together: worship of the Lord cannot be separated from treatment due to the poor and weak. Amos, coming from Tecoa, was sent to Bethel to confront a religious, prosperous and morally corrupted people. The book alternates oracles of judgment, solemn warnings, and, at the end, a hope of restoration.
profile.setting: The backdrop is the northern kingdom, Israel, after the division of the kingdom in 931 BC, when Jeroboam I established shrines in Dan and Bethel to ward off the people of Jerusalem. These centers of worship have become marked by a mixture of worship of the Lord with idolatrous practices, including images of calves and the presence of the baals. Amos works at Bethel, probably just before 753 BC, in a period of political and economic prosperity both in Israel and Judah, but also of increasing oppression of the poor by the rich. The introduction points out that authorship is attributed to Amos himself, although his image is not that of a professional prophet; the date and duration of the ministry are treated as probable, not absolute.

structure.label: Prologue and initial accusation
structure.description: Brief opening that places the prophetic word and introduces the mission of Amos before Israel.

structure.label: Indictments against the nations and against Israel
structure.description: Series of accusations that first affect neighboring peoples and culminate in the direct accusation against Israel.

structure.label: Warnings, questions and signs of judgment
structure.description: Messages that accuse Israel's guilt, expose their false security and announce the imminent danger, with resources such as rhetorical questions, irony and historical memories.

structure.label: Laments and woe against false trust
structure.description: Called to repentance and warnings against trust in the day of the Lord, in wealth, in houses and fortifications.

structure.label: Visions of judgment and promise of restoration
structure.description: Series of visions showing unavoidable judgments, interrupted by a biographical picture, and ended with the fall of Israel and a final promise of reconstruction and restoration.

themes: The Union of True Worship and Social Justice
The condemnation of the oppression of the poor and the abuse of power
God's judgment on false religious and material security
The responsibility of the covenant people before the revelation of God
readingKeys: Notice how the book links religious sin and social sin: idolatry and injustice appear as parts of the same problem.
Notice the change of focus: Amos begins by judging the nations around, but he turns attention to Israel and Judah.
Read the final visions as the climax of the prophetic argument: they intensify the judgment before they make room for the promise of restoration.
profile.cautions: The introduction does not feature Amos as a prophet of office, but also does not describe it simply as a miserable peasant; the source suggests that he probably had some patrimony and administrative experience. The exact date of ministry is approximate, and the duration is uncertain. Although the book ends with hope, this does not soften the seriousness of the denunciations: the restoration comes after the confrontation with the real sin of the people.

dossier.narratedEra: The book places its main action in the kingdom of North (Israel) and, to a lesser extent, in Judah, during the period of Jeroboam II in Israel and Uzziah/Azarias in Judah, before the fall of Israel to Assyria. The narrated setting includes the royal sanctuary of Bethel, the cities of Samaria, Jerusalem and borders marked by Aryan, Philistia, Tyre, Edom and Ammon. The notes also evoke a broader horizon of judgment and restoration, with reference to exile, devastation and return to the land.
dossier.compositionEra: The sources provided treat Amos as a message received by visionary revelation and uttered by a man of Judah called tekoinha/surer, not as a professional prophet. The date of ministry is placed just before 753 BC, perhaps for a single year, in the reign of Jeroboam II, with allusions to an earthquake at the time of Uzziah. Matthew Henry's introduction reflects a traditional devotional reading without proposing an alternative date of distinct composition from the setting, while Tyndale notes distinguish the prophet's vocation and the historical context in which the message was delivered.

politics.title: Division between Israel and Judah
politics.detail: After the division of the kingdom in 931 BC, North (Israel) and the South (Juda) followed different political and religious paths. Jeroboam I created rival centers of worship in Dan and Bethel to prevent the subjects of the North from going to Jerusalem.
politics.readingImpact: Amos' criticism of Bethel worship reaches an established political and religious structure, not just individual sins. This helps to read your complaint as a confrontation to the Northern Kingdom system.

politics.title: Jeroboam II and the height of Israel
politics.detail: Amos is situated just before the death of Jeroboam II (753 BC). The notes link this period to an expansion obtained in a vacuum of power: Assyria had captured Damascus, but retreated, and Egypt was in decline. Israel and Judah prospered and resumed part of the lost territory.
politics.readingImpact: National prosperity explains why warnings against wealth, luxury and abuse of the poor sound so urgent: economic growth has increased the oppression of the vulnerable.

politics.title: Assyria as a threat and instrument of judgment
politics.detail: The notes recall the capture of Damascus by Assyria around 801 BC and the fall of the Northern kingdom in 722 BC as the fulfillment of the announcement of judgment. They also mention the definitive weakening of peoples as the Philistines under Assyrian pressure.
politics.readingImpact: The reading of Amos gains historical weight: his words are not only moralizing, but are part of a conjuncture in which empires reshape the region and make the catastrophe announced plausible.

politics.title: Bethel as a centre of cultual and judicial dispute
politics.detail: The Bethel sanctuary appears as the main place of ministry of Amos (7:13) and as the likely target of judgment in 9:1. The introduction presents it as real Northern shrines associated with the distortion of the cult; 9:1 shows the judgment starting at the center of worship.
politics.readingImpact: Bethel is not a neutral scenario: it is the institutional heart of the Northern cult. This intensifies the denunciation that the official religion was corrupted and would be judged first.

politics.title: Disputes with neighboring nations
politics.detail: The oracles against Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom and Ammon describe wars, slave trade, treason of alliances and extreme violence. Damascus is remembered for brutality in Gilead; Gaza and Tyre for selling captives; Edom for persistent aggression; Ammon for cruelty of war.
politics.readingImpact: The first block of Amos creates the listener's agreement against external enemies, before reaccusing Israel. This makes the internal complaint sound more convincing and inevitable.

customs.title: Cult with images, altars and syncretism
customs.detail: The notes describe the use of golden calves in Dan and Bethel, and the presence of baalins as a cult parallel to the LORD. Amos' message combats a religion in which Yahweh was worshipped alongside local deities to obtain rain, fertility or other benefits.
customs.readingImpact: Amos' criticism is the mixed cult, not just the lack of ritual. Reading becomes clearer when one sees that public faith has been shaped by pragmatic and idolatrous interests.

customs.title: Unequal economic life and legal abuse
customs.detail: The notes speak of a time when the rich became richer and the poor poorest. In 5:10-13, the courts are described as controlled by the rich, with corrupt judges and contracted witnesses; in 5:11, stone houses contrast with brick dwellings of the peasants.
customs.readingImpact: Amos should be read as a concrete social denunciation: sin includes legal exploitation, material inequality and manipulation of truth against the weak.

customs.title: Meals, parties and self-satisfaction
customs.detail: Section 4:1-3 is summarized as an accusation of the "turm of the feast," that is, to the self-indulgents. In 5:18:14, the target are those who trust in wealth, houses, and fortifications, suggesting an elite that surrounds themselves with comfort and safety.
customs.readingImpact: Readers should not only imagine private luxury, but a culture of celebration and self-confidence incompatible with divine judgment.

customs.title: Practices of grief and funeral poetry
customs.detail: In 5:1-3, Amós sings a qinah, a funerary lamentation with special rhythm (3+2). The comment explains that the country is treated as if it were already dead, awaiting burial.
customs.readingImpact: Gender changes reading: it is not only a threat; it is a prophetic lament that declares the social and spiritual death of Israel before historical destruction.

customs.title: Rural work, creation and fig trees of sycamore
customs.detail: Amos is described as noqed and in 7:14, as boqer; the notes discuss that this may indicate possession and administration of herds and cattle, not just an employee's service. He also "cuidava" of sycamores, whose fruits were used for animal forage.
customs.readingImpact: This alters the image of the prophet: he does not necessarily appear as a miserable peasant, but as someone connected to the rural world and perhaps of a certain status, whose voice goes with authority to the North.

language.title: Prophetic formula and revelation by visions
language.detail: The expression "words" in 1:1 is presented as a default way of introducing prophetic message. The notes also say that Amos received the message in visions, that is, by divine revelation.
language.readingImpact: The book is presented as an authorized communication of God, not as a generic religious opinion; the reader must listen to the oracular form with literary and theological seriousness.

language.title: Repetition three... and up to four
language.detail: In 1:3, the formula three crimes, and up to four" is explained as a pattern of repeated rebellion, does not count exact mathematics.
language.readingImpact: Language intensifies the moral weight of national sins and prevents the literalistic reading of the formula; the focus is the accumulation of guilt.

language.title: Image of thream and crushing
language.detail: In 1:3, the violence of Damascus is compared to the process of threw grains with iron/aphyation teeth sled, an image of extreme brutality.
language.readingImpact: The metaphor makes the cruelty concrete and corporal; the divine judgment responds to a violence that dehumanizes.

language.title: Phrases-hino on the Creator
language.detail: The hymnic fragments of 4:13; 5:8-9; 9:5-6 emphasize that the LORD created and rules constellations, water, and cosmos, in contrast to local gods.
language.readingImpact: Amos broadens the horizon: the God who judges Israel is the universal Lord of creation, not a regional divinity.

language.title: Word game and prophetic irony
language.detail: The notes point to alliterations and puns at 5:5 (Gilgal... exile), sarcasm in 4:4-5 and irony when treating sacrifices as an attempt at magic manipulation rather than repentance.
language.readingImpact: These resources show that prophecy is not only direct denunciation; it exposes the self-contradiction of worship and national security.

language.title: The Day of the LORD as a reversal of expectation
language.detail: In 5:18-20, the day of the LORD is explained as divine intervention for righteousness, but in Amos it becomes a dark day for a guilty people.
language.readingImpact: The known vocabulary of the cult gets new meaning: expectation of national victory is reversed in a trial announcement.

timeline.title: 931 BC: division of the kingdom
timeline.detail: The united monarchy is divided into Israel (north) and Judah (south). Jeroboam I institutes alternative shrines in Dan and Bethel.
timeline.readingImpact: This milestone explains why Amos concentrates his criticism on the cult of the North and why Bethel becomes a symbol of infidelity.

timeline.title: c. 843792 BC: reign of Hazael and Benhadad in Damascus
timeline.detail: The notes date Hazael as a usurper and Ben-hadad as his successor; Damascus appears as an aggressor power against Israel.
timeline.readingImpact: Helps read the oracles against Damascus as a judgment on already known regional violence of listeners.

timeline.title: c. 801 BC: Assyrian shock and regional turnaround
timeline.detail: Assyria captures Damascus, but then withdraws from trouble elsewhere; this vacuum favors the prosperity of Israel and Judah.
timeline.readingImpact: The prosperity denounced by Amos appears as historically contingent and politically dangerous, not as an automatic sign of divine favor.

timeline.title: c. 793-753 BC: Jeroboam II and Uzziah/Azarias
timeline.detail: The notes are Jeroboam II (793-753 BC) in Israel and Uzziah/Azarias (792-740 BC) in Judah, with mention of the earthquake of the time of Uzziah as an event of judgment.
timeline.readingImpact: The time setting concentrates Amos' ministry in a period of political force and apparent stability, which the prophecy denies.

timeline.title: Shortly before 753 BC: brief ministry at Bethel
timeline.detail: The introduction states that the ministry of Amos was brief, perhaps restricted to a year, in the royal sanctuary of Bethel, just before the death of Jeroboam II.
timeline.readingImpact: The brevity of the ministry accentuates the urgency of the message and the risk taken by the prophet in confronting the Northern religious center.

timeline.title: 722 BC: fall of the kingdom of the North
timeline.detail: Assyria conquers the kingdom of the North in 722 BC, presented as a fulfillment of Amos' warning on the day of darkness and the dispersion of Israel.
timeline.readingImpact: The reading of the book gains a retrospective dimension: its threats did not stay in the air, but connect to Israel's historical outcome.

investigation: The available sources mainly cover the introduction and notes of Amos 1, 5 and 9; therefore, several aspects of the book are known only selectively.

Matthew Henry's tradition reads Amos as a prophet of Judah who speaks above all against Israel and closes with Messianic promise; Tyndale highlights his historical context, his non-professional vocation and his social criticism.
There is an interpretative proposal, not demonstrated as an independent historical fact, that Amos was not a poor shepherd, but someone with possession or administration of herds and sycamorees.
The exact place of the altar in 9:1 is discussed in the notes: it may be the Bethel sanctuary or the temple of Jerusalem.
The notes deal with names, puns and poetic images as real literary elements of the text, but avoid fixing etymologies or certainly identify some gods and places mentioned in 5:26-27 and 1:5.
There is no complete chronology of writing the book in the sources; the material received speaks of the period of prophecy and interpretive tradition, not a detailed editorial process.
dossier.limits: This dossier was built only with the notes provided by Tyndale and Matthew Henry; I did not use external data or complete gaps with their own knowledge. Therefore, the coverage is necessarily partial and tends to emphasize the excerpts commented on the attached sources. Some statements appear only as an interpretation of the commentators, especially on social status of Amos, identification of gods at 5:26-27, and the site of the altar in 9:1; such items were marked as interpretation or debated when the source itself indicated uncertainty. It was also not possible to develop in detail themes of the book that were not dealt directly in the annexed notes, such as most of the specific accusations of chapters 2-4 and 6-8. The distinction between historical setting and date of composition was preserved as requested: what the sources clearly affirm is the context of the prophetic ministry and the subsequent theological reading, not an extensive editorial theory.
